result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.to_prufer_sequence()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Encode an undirected tree as its Prüfer sequence. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L47255-L47326){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.to_prufer_sequence() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![To Prüfer sequence](/assets/graphs/to-prufer-sequence.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A tree on node ids 1 to 6: 3–1, 1–5, 5–2, 5–6, and 6–4. Repeatedly removing the smallest leaf and writing down its neighbor removes 2, 3, 1, and 4 in that order (filled order badges), along the four edges in the accent color; removing 3 turns 1 into a leaf, so it goes next. The card shows the removed leaves and the returned sequence [5, 1, 5, 6]." width="100%"} The Prüfer sequence is a compact code for a labeled tree: a tree on `n` nodes becomes a list of `n - 2` node IDs, and every such list decodes back to exactly one tree. It is built by repeatedly removing the smallest leaf and writing down its neighbor. The correspondence proves Cayley's formula (there are $n^{n-2}$ labeled trees), and it is handy for storing trees compactly, for generating uniformly random trees (draw a random sequence), and for genetic algorithms that evolve trees. "Smallest" refers to node IDs in ascending order. A node appears in the sequence once for every neighbor it has beyond the first, so leaves never appear. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The `n - 2` node IDs of the sequence. Rebuild the tree with `Graph.from_prufer_sequence()`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed, has fewer than two nodes, or is not a tree. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The encoder runs in $O(n)$ time with the linear-time scheme also used by NetworkX: a pointer moves up through the node IDs looking for the next leaf, except when removing a leaf turns its neighbor into a leaf with a smaller ID, which is then taken right away. NetworkX numbers nodes `0` to `n - 1`; here the nodes are ranked by ID, so on a graph whose IDs are `1` to `n` the sequence matches NetworkX's shifted by one. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a star, every leaf hangs off the center, so the center is written down `n - 2` times: ::: {#c330aa3e .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec star = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["hub", "a", "b", "c", "d"]) star.add_edges([("hub", "a"), ("hub", "b"), ("hub", "c"), ("hub", "d")]) [star.get_label_from_id(n) for n in star.to_prufer_sequence()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['hub', 'hub', 'hub'] ``` ::: ::: A path writes down each inner node once: ::: {#97c6d473 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} path = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]) path.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E")]) [path.get_label_from_id(n) for n in path.to_prufer_sequence()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['B', 'C', 'D'] ``` ::: :::
